reason: I found a real defect, checked whether the project has already ruled on that exact defect, and it has, in the proposer's favour, so I do not refute. THE DEFECT: Taylor does not end the fifth line with a full stop. He ends it with a COLON, and the sentence runs on, Withdrawn to the mountains, a crownless king: / Whence, ever retreating, he sends again / Impotent showers of sleet that darkle / In belts across the green o' the plain. I confirmed the colon in two independent witnesses, Project Gutenberg 14591 at text line 1875 and the Wikisource transcription of Goethe's Faust (Taylor), Scene 2, at its line 192. So the closing full stop in the shipped quotation is an editorial substitution, not Taylor. THE PRECEDENT: this is the same substitution the March Hamlet candidate made (Folger ends For use almost can change the stamp of nature with a comma and runs on), the March refuter examined it in 03-poet-01 and wrote that the cut is at a complete clause and adds no word, so I do not count it as minting; and the curator here disclosed it in the same place and almost the same words, Taylor ends line 5 with a colon and the sentence runs on, so the closing full stop is the cut, at a complete clause. It is disclosed, it is at a clause boundary, and it adds no word, so by the project's own settled handling it stands. It is NOT the 03-phil-10 case, where the shipped mark differed from the named edition INSIDE the quotation and revealed the wrong edition underneath; here every mark inside the quotation is Taylor's. The editor who wants no substituted mark at all has one faithful alternative, which is to run the quotation to Taylor's own full stop at In belts across the green o' the plain., eight lines instead of five, at the cost of ending on sleet in a renewal month. EVERYTHING ELSE HOLDS. Wording: the five lines match both witnesses word for word, with the American colors, the semicolon after Spring, the commas after cling and shiver and after mountains, and the capitals at each line head, so rule 7 is satisfied. Locator: the file's table of contents reads II. BEFORE THE CITY-GATE, the scene heading at text line 1667 reads BEFORE THE CITY-GATE, the sub-heading FAUST AND WAGNER stands at 1866 and the speech prefix FAUST at 1869, so the lines open Faust's Easter-walk speech to Wagner, as the source says. The German is Vom Eise befreit sind Strom und Bäche, lines 903 to 907 by the standard numbering; the verifier was right to leave numbers he had not checked out of the source. Translator and year: Bayard Taylor, Part One first published 1870, which matches the landed March card's Part Two 1871. Attribution: Goethe, in Faust's mouth, speaker named, and this is not the Anster Boldness has genius trap that the misattribution list warns about in this very poem. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, not banned, Goethe yearCount 1 (March), so this is his second of three. FORM: source leads with the name, no dash, no straight double quote, 102 characters, tag Drama correct and consistent with the March Faust card. In scope, publishable, and on the month's theme as directly as anything in the batch. TWO NOTES FOR THE EDITOR. First, this is a second Faust line in Bayard Taylor in consecutive months; no rule forbids it, but the year will read thin if Goethe's third is also Faust. Second, the source names no scene number while the March card does name Act V, scene 6; betterCitation adds Taylor's own scene II and still fits, at 111 characters.
